name: Combat
content:
ENTERING COMBAT

When combat or some other tense situation arises and it becomes necessary to track the action carefully, special rules apply governing characters' actions.

GROUP COMBATANTS

Start by dividing the participants into GROUPS. Each round will include a turn for each group to take action, with members of each group acting in whatever order they choose within that group's turn.

At a minimum there should be two groups (party members and foes), but depending on the situation, there may also be one or more groups of allies, additional foes, non-combatants and/or environmental factors (like a collapsing roof or an erupting volcano). The GM can divide or combine these additional groups as they choose for the purpose of determining initiative:

INITIATIVE

To determine the INITIATIVE order among the groups, each member of each group rolls one feat die (d12) and adds their WITS score to the result. Add together the highest result and lowest result among the group to determine that group’s total initiative result.

Then compare all groups' results to determine the initiative order for the encounter. If there is a tie, each tied group rolls a single feat die as a tiebreaker.

SURPRISE

Any character who rolls a Sol 🌞 on their initiative roll gets to act in a surprise round: a separate round of actions that happens before the regular initiative takes effect. Note that only the character that rolled the Sol 🌞 - not their whole group - gets to act in the surprise round. Also note that any number of characters from any number of groups may act in the surprise round. Compare individual initiative rolls to determine the order of action in the surprise round.

Any character who rolls Morte 💀 on their initiative roll is caught off guard and may not take action during the first regular round of combat.

If the party wants to ambush or otherwise get the drop on their foes, treat it as a group skill check, as outlined in the Core Stats section. On a success, the whole group gets to act in the surprise round.

ROUNDS OF COMBAT

When acting in combat, each round represents about 5 seconds and consists of one turn for each participating group. When it is a group’s turn to act, each member of the group takes a turn - in whatever order they choose among themselves - before moving on to the next group.

TAKING ACTION

Each combatant may MOVE, up to their speed, and take ACTIONS and HALF ACTIONS on their turn. By default, characters have 1 ½ actions per turn, but there are many traits and effects that can increase or reduce that number.

They may also take one or more FREE ACTIONS on their turn, such as brief communication, gestures, or simple interactions with objects, like opening or closing a door, pulling a lever, picking up or dropping an item, sheathing or pulling out a weapon, etc.

Finally, they also have a REACTION available to them if they have an ability that allows them to use it. These are generally triggered by specific events and can be used at any time in combat, regardless of which group or combatant is acting currently.

Abilities define whether they require an action, half action, free action or reaction.

In addition to your explicit abilities, you can make skill checks on your turn. Some examples: Using Stealth to hide; Using Awe to intimidate foes; Using Craft to improvise a barricade. The GM is responsible for determining what can be reasonably accomplished through a skill check on a combat turn, whether it costs an action or half action, what is an appropriate TN and what effects a success or failure might produce.

MOVEMENT, PRONE & FALLING

You can break up your movement on your turn, moving before, after or in between actions. Any combination is fine as long as your total movement for the turn is within your speed.

Climbing, crawling, swimming, navigating difficult terrain and any other inhibited movement all costs twice as much movement to accomplish. For example, swimming through 10 feet of water requires 20 feet of movement.

You may choose to spend one action on your turn to sprint, doubling your speed for the turn. You can only spend one action in this way per turn.

In general, you're able to move through space occupied by allies, but not through space occupied by foes or other obstacles. The GM has discretion to determine where a character can and cannot move.

Combatants who are able to fly are able to move through the air up to their speed, but if they are knocked prone, their speed is reduced to 0, or they are otherwise made unable to move, they fall to the ground.

While prone, you automatically lose Engagements, your attack rolls are ill-favored and ranged attacks against you from further away than short range are ill-favored. To stand up from prone, you must spend half your movement on your turn. Otherwise, your only movement option is to crawl. You may fall prone on your turn as a free action.

FALLING, JUMPING, LIFTING, PUSHING, PULLING

Falling to the ground from a height deals 1d6 for every 10 feet fallen. Additionally, for every 20 feet fallen, roll Injury. For example, a character who falls from a height of 40 feet would take 4d6 damage and roll Injury twice.

You can jump a distance equal to your height from a standing position, or twice that distance with a running start of at least 10 feet. Either way, the maximum height of your jump is half your height, and the jump distance counts as movement.

You can lift, push or pull objects weighing up to your own weight.

The GM may allow you to exceed these limits with a successful skill check.

REACH & OPPORTUNITY ATTACKS

By default, combatants control a 5 foot square in combat and their Reach extends to the 5 foot squares adjacent to their own. Larger or smaller combatants may take up more or less space and have longer or shorter Reach.

Abilities and equipment that augment Reach or provide their own extend a character's existing Reach. For example, a combatant with standard Reach who is wielding a polearm with Reach: 5 is able to engage with foes in squares one beyond those adjacent to their own.

Whenever one combatant leaves another's Reach, the latter may use their Reaction to make a single melee attack against them, immediately.

DRAG, SHOVE & GRAPPLE

Attempting to drag, shove or grapple with a foe is generally resolved via an opposed skill check. Having a foe in a grapple generally means that attacks against them are favored and that they must break out of the grapple (via another opposed skill check on their turn) in order to move. However, the GM has full discretion to adjudicate these actions.

EVADE & COVER

On your turn, you may spend one action to Evade. If you do, choose one:

  • You avoid opportunity attacks this turn.

  • Until your next turn, attacks against you from combatants you can see are ill-favored and your Dexterity checks are favored.

If a significant obstacle stands between an attacker and a target, the GM may choose to make an attack ill-favored, apply one or more -d penalties, or disallow the attack entirely. They may also require a skill check to determine how well a combatant can position themselves behind cover.

DELAYING

You have the option to delay your entire turn or part of your turn. To do so, declare a specific event that will trigger your delayed turn or specific part of your turn (movement, part of your movement, one or more actions or half actions) and describe what you intend to do (i.e. "I will run to the door if the ogre moves away from it.").

When the trigger happens, you automatically take your turn (or part of your turn) immediately.

If at the end of the round the trigger has not happened, if you delayed your whole turn, take your turn. If you only delayed part of your turn, that part is forfeited. Either way, after completing your delayed turn or part of your turn, you rejoin your group in the initiative order for the next round.

HELP

You may spend one action on your turn to pass a +1d bonus to an ally on a relevant check this round, per GM discretion. Describe how you're helping them.

ATTACKS & DAMAGE

Any ability that inflicts harm or imposes the will of another on one or more combatants is considered an ATTACK. Attacks can employ many different mechanics, but most follow two common patterns:

  • The attacker rolls a skill check against a difficulty equal to one of the target’s stats (Defense is the default for physical attacks).

  • The attacker and target each make skill checks in opposition to each other.

Attacks have a wide range of effects when successful, but many attacks call for a damage roll.

DAMAGE ROLLS

The type and number of dice to include in a damage roll, as well as what modifiers to add to the result, are defined by the ability and/or weapon used. The result of a damage roll is always subtracted from the target’s current Endurance.

There are no explicit damage types in Renaissance, but if the nature of the damage is relevant to the situation, the GM can award bonuses or impose penalties at their discretion, generally adding or removing dice from the pool for the damage roll, or doubling/halving the total damage.

See the Dice Rolls section.

MELEE ATTACKS & ENGAGEMENT

Melee combat is rarely a simple case of taking a swing with a weapon. More often, there is an exchange of careful maneuvers and footwork before an attacker attempts to land a blow. This exchange is represented by ENGAGEMENT.

Any time a combatant makes a melee attack, they and the target of their attack each make engagement rolls to determine the outcome of the exchange.

Each character has a number of engagement dice available to them each round. These dice are generally granted by equipment they're carrying and by their martial training. As such, combatants specializing in melee combat are likely to have far more engagement dice than those who specialize in other areas.

Each combatant chooses how many of their engagement dice to roll for each engagement. Since they are a per-round resource, in some situations it may be advantageous to reserve some dice for other engagements. The number and types of the dice you’re committing to the engagement do not have to be declared before rolling. In fact, any and all methods of concealing your dice - or even deceptive tactics like shaking dice in your hand but not actually rolling them - are fair game.

Once both sides have chosen their dice, count down from three and then roll all engagement dice simultaneously. Compare the highest result from each side, then compare the next-highest pair, then the next-highest, etc. If one combatant rolls more dice than the other, the unopposed dice count as wins. If one side decides not to roll any engagement dice, they automatically lose the engagement. If neither side rolled any dice, it's a tie.

As you resolve each pair of engagement dice, describe the action and - at the end - how it positions the attacker to strike a blow.

Once engagement is resolved, the attacker makes their attack roll. If the attacker won more engagement pairs, the attack roll is favored. If the defender won more pairs, the attack roll is ill-favored. If there is a tie, the attack is unmodified.

Unless a weapon or ability states otherwise, attack rolls for melee weapons are always Strength vs Defense and on a hit the weapon deals its damage, plus your BODY score, reducing the foe's current Endurance.

The 9 and 7 are the highest for each combatant, so we compare them and the attacker wins that pair. The 5 and 3 are the next-highest, so we compare them and, once again, the attacker wins. The remaining d6 from the attacker is unopposed, so that's another win. That's a 3-0 engagement victory for the attacker, so their attack roll is favored.

ENGAGEMENT SUCCESSES

Any time you roll the maximum number on an engagement die, it is an ENGAGEMENT SUCCESS, which you can spend to achieve various effects. The effects available to you are determined by your martial training and by the equipment you're currently wielding. Each ability or equipment item indicates which engagement success effects it contributes. Below are all available effects:

  • BIND - You and your opponent's weapons lock together. The engagement ends in a draw, immediately (the attack still proceeds).

  • COMPASS - You move around your opponent to any position adjacent to them.

  • DISARM - Your opponent drops a wielded item of your choosing. You may only use this if you have already used another success in this engagement.

  • FEINT  - You may reroll one of your engagement dice.

  • HOOK - Choose one piece of your opponent's armor or their shield. They lose the benefits of that item until their next turn.

  • INVITATION - Your opponent must reroll an engagement die of your choice.

  • KNOCKBACK - You push your opponent 5 feet back. The attacker in this engagement must spend additional movement to maintain melee range. Otherwise, the engagement ends and no attack is made. If this is the second time you've used Knockback in this engagement, the opponent is also knocked prone.

  • MANCHETTE - You land a glancing blow. Your opponent takes 1 injury.

  • PARRY - You deflect your opponent's incoming attack. You win this pair, regardless of who has the higher die result. If your opponent also uses Parry for this pair, the higher die result wins as normal.

  • RETREAT - You move 5 feet away from your opponent. The attacker in this engagement must spend additional movement to regain melee range. Otherwise, the engagement ends and no attack is made.

  • RIPOSTE - Make a melee attack against your opponent immediately, skipping engagement, then return to this engagement. You may only use this if you have already used another success in this engagement.

  • STUN - All of your opponent's engagement dice become spent (even those not used in this engagement).

  • SUNDER - Choose one piece of your opponent's armor or their shield. That item grants 1 less Defense, permanently. If they have no armor or shield, or only natural armor, their current Defense is reduced by 1.

You don't have to match specific engagement dice with their specific success effects. The available effects are pooled together and can be bought with successes from any of your engagement dice.

For example, let's say you're wielding a shield that grants you 1d4 engagement and the Parry success effect, as well as a war hammer that grants you 1d6 engagement and the Knockback success effect. If you were to roll a 4 on the d4 or a 6 on the d6, you could spend that success on either Parry OR Knockback.

RANGE & RANGED ATTACKS

Many abilities and equipment items have a Range, which is expressed in four tiers:

Adjacent = squares adjacent to your own.
Short Range = up to 25 feet
Medium Range = up to 50 feet
Long Range = up to 100 feet
Far Range = up to 200 feet

By default, ranged attacks are always Dexterity vs Defense and on a hit the weapon deals its damage, plus your BODY score, reducing the foe's current Endurance.

Ranged attacks against adjacent foes are ill-favored if the foe can see you.

For attacks that have a range of Short Range or higher, if the attack roll is not already ill-favored, you may make it ill-favored to double its range.

INJURY

INFLICTING INJURY

An exceptionally well-aimed attack can inflict INJURY on its target, raising the target’s Injury score and making them more susceptible to the Helpless state. Some abilities may provide special ways of inflicting Injury, but by default, if the skill check for the attack has a Sol 🌞 on the feat die, the attacker inflicts an Injury on the target (even if the overall attack roll total is below the difficulty).

One exception to this is in cases where the target gets an opposing skill check. In that case, if the target rolls Sol 🌞 on the feat die for the opposing check, this prevents the attack from inflicting Injury.

Whenever Injury is inflicted, the target rolls a feat die:

  • On a 1-10, the result is added to the target’s current Injury score.

  • On Sol ☀️, the wound is insignificant - no Injury is inflicted.

  • On Morte 💀, the wound is dire - the target’s Injury score increases to equal their maximum Defense.

Alternately, the target may choose to resist the Injury:

RESISTING INJURY

If an attack inflicts Injury on a target and they are not Helpless, before rolling for Injury, a combatant may choose to resist the Injury by checking a Condition: they heighten their emotions to avoid the worst of a blow. If they do so, they may roll two feat dice instead of one for their Injury roll and keep the more favorable result.

DEATH

KNOCKOUTS & DYING

When your Endurance is reduced to 0, you are knocked unconscious. You fall prone and drop any items you’re carrying that aren’t attached to your body.

While unconscious, your Defense is reduced by 10 + WITS. Armor and any other effects augmenting your Defense remain in place.

If you are not Helpless, you wake up after an hour with 1 Endurance. If you are Helpless and unconscious, you are dying: if you don’t return to at least 1 Endurance within an hour, you die.

Any character may attempt to stabilize someone who is dying by making an Aid check. The difficulty is equal to the dying person’s current Injury score + 10. On a success, they remain at 0 Endurance but are no longer dying. They must regain at least 1 Endurance to wake up.

Any time you wake up from being knocked unconscious, check a Condition.

It is possible to die instantly. When damage reduces you to 0 Endurance and there is damage remaining, you die instantly if the remaining damage equals or exceeds your Endurance maximum.

If an attacker wants to knock a foe unconscious without risk of killing them, they must declare this intent before making their attack roll. If they reduce the foe to 0 Endurance, the foe falls unconscious, is stable, and will wake up in one hour with 1 Endurance.

SUFFOCATION

A character can hold their breath for a number of seconds equal to twice their maximum Endurance, rounded up to the nearest 5 seconds. Once that limit is reached, they lose half their current Endurance, rounded up, each turn. If they reach 0 Endurance, follow the normal rules for knockouts and dying.
